Even elite senior engineers and system architects occasionally encounter unfamiliar questions during high-stakes technical interviews, particularly when dealing with complex, multi-layered domains like Exception Handling and non-blocking I/O (NIO). When an interviewer probes into a niche mechanic—such as the exact readiness selection states of a Selector or the nuanced thread-safety guarantees of a buffer flip operation—guessing or bluffing is an immediate disqualifier. The key is to manage the unknown systematically by breaking down the problem using first principles, transparently communicating your mental model, and mapping known concepts to the unfamiliar domain. 

In the context of low-level I/O and exception flows, handling an unknown question requires you to anchor your response in architectural invariants. If you do not know a specific API method or low-level kernel detail, demonstrate how you would investigate it, what edge cases you would anticipate (like buffer underflows, socket exhaustion, or selector blocking behavior), and how you design resilient systems around failure boundaries. Interviewers are rarely testing rote memorization; they are evaluating your diagnostic reasoning under pressure, your intellectual humility, and your engineering problem-solving methodology when standard patterns break down.

items: Acknowledge the gap immediately and honestly without making excuses, pivoting swiftly to how you deconstruct unfamiliar technical problems.
Deconstruct the problem by identifying familiar boundary conditions, such as distinguishing between blocking socket channels and non-blocking selector loops.
Formulate a reasoned hypothesis based on first principles of operating system I/O multiplexing, memory allocation, and exception propagation.
Collaborate with the interviewer by treating the interview as a pair-debugging session, asking targeted clarifying questions about scale, concurrency, or constraints.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Interview Insight: Technical leads respect engineers who say 'I haven't encountered this specific edge case in production, but based on how Java NIO Selectors handle epoll registration, my approach would be...' far more than those who try to mask their ignorance with confident jargon. Always pivot from what you do not know to the rigorous framework you use to figure things out.

title: How do you handle a question you do not know in interview?
